title: Palpitations: Capture the Rhythm Before You Name It
bottomLine: Palpitations are a symptom, not a rhythm diagnosis. First identify instability/red flags, obtain an ECG when possible, then match ambulatory monitoring duration to symptom frequency so intermittent arrhythmias are documented rather than guessed from symptom description alone.
recognize: Palpitations can reflect premature beats, SVT, AF/flutter, ventricular arrhythmia, sinus tachycardia, medication/substance effects or nonarrhythmic awareness of heartbeat.
Syncope, exertional symptoms, structural heart disease, family history of sudden death or an abnormal ECG increase arrhythmic risk.
differentiate: A regular abrupt-onset/offset episode suggests re-entrant SVT more than sinus tachycardia, but symptom pattern alone does not prove the mechanism.
Anxiety can coexist with arrhythmia and should not be used to close the differential before basic cardiac assessment.
assessment: Characterize onset/offset, regularity, duration, triggers, exertion, chest pain, dyspnea, presyncope/syncope and pulse rate if known.
Review stimulants, decongestants, thyroid medication, alcohol/cannabis, QT-prolonging drugs and family history of cardiomyopathy/sudden death.
workup: Obtain 12-lead ECG and targeted CBC/electrolyte/thyroid testing when clinically indicated.
Use Holter, patch/event monitor or longer-term monitoring based on symptom frequency and risk; echocardiography is appropriate when structural disease is suspected.
management: Treat the documented rhythm and underlying trigger rather than palpitations generically.
Urgently refer sustained tachyarrhythmia with instability, exertional syncope, wide-complex tachycardia or significant structural disease.
medicationSafety: Do not start rate-slowing therapy blindly in unexplained palpitations with baseline bradycardia/conduction disease.
Correct electrolyte/drug contributors to QT prolongation when present.
counselling: Teach patients to record timing, pulse/rhythm if feasible, triggers and associated symptoms; explain why rhythm capture changes treatment.
followUp: Review ambulatory-monitor results and ensure significant arrhythmias reach cardiology/electrophysiology pathways.
examTrap: Diagnosing panic disorder from palpitations before obtaining an ECG/risk history—or prescribing a beta blocker before the rhythm is known.
oneLinePearl: Palpitations are solved by rhythm capture, not by adjectives.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/CHRS atrial fibrillation clinical evaluation guidance

title: Cardiomyopathy: Define the Phenotype, Then Search for Cause and Risk
bottomLine: Cardiomyopathy is not synonymous with reduced EF. Define the structural/functional phenotype, search for reversible or inherited causes, assess arrhythmic/sudden-death risk, and manage heart-failure physiology while arranging cardiology/genetic/specialty care when indicated.
recognize: Dilated, hypertrophic, arrhythmogenic and restrictive phenotypes have different causes and risk profiles.
Presentation may be heart failure, murmur, arrhythmia, syncope, embolic event or an incidental abnormal ECG/echo.
differentiate: Ischemic heart disease, severe valve disease and long-standing hypertension can produce ventricular dysfunction but require cause-specific framing.
Athlete's heart can mimic hypertrophy; unexplained wall thickness, family history or abnormal ECG warrants cardiomyopathy evaluation.
assessment: Assess HF symptoms, syncope/presyncope, palpitations, chest pain, family history of cardiomyopathy/sudden death, pregnancy/postpartum status, alcohol/toxins and chemotherapy exposure.
Review neuromuscular/systemic disease and prior myocarditis/infection clues.
workup: Use ECG and echocardiography as core tests; cardiac MRI adds tissue characterization and morphology when indicated.
Use ischemic evaluation, labs and genetic/family screening according to phenotype and cardiology guidance.
management: Treat congestion and guideline-directed HF physiology when present while addressing the specific cardiomyopathy.

Refer hypertrophic/arrhythmogenic/inherited disease and unexplained nonischemic cardiomyopathy for specialist risk stratification, genetic counselling/testing and device consideration where appropriate.
medicationSafety: Some cardiomyopathies are preload/outflow sensitive; avoid assuming generic HF medications are equally appropriate before phenotype is defined.
Pregnancy/postpartum cardiomyopathy changes medication choices and requires coordinated obstetric-cardiology care.
counselling: Discuss exercise and family screening only after phenotype/risk is clarified; avoid blanket restrictions without specialist context.
followUp: Track EF/function, symptoms, arrhythmias and family/genetic evaluation; ensure device/referral decisions are closed-loop.
examTrap: Calling any low EF 'dilated cardiomyopathy' without evaluating ischemia, valve disease, toxins or inherited causes.
oneLinePearl: Cardiomyopathy management starts with phenotype and cause, not EF alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart-failure/cardiomyopathy practice resources

title: Stress Testing: Match the Test to the Question and the Patient
bottomLine: Stress testing is useful only when pretest probability and the clinical question make the result actionable. Choose exercise ECG, stress echo or nuclear/imaging stress based on baseline ECG interpretability, exercise capacity, comorbidity and local expertise; do not order stress testing for active ACS or very low-risk nonspecific symptoms.
recognize: Exercise capacity and symptoms during testing add prognostic information beyond the ECG alone.
Baseline LBBB, paced rhythm, significant ST abnormalities or inability to exercise can make plain exercise ECG inappropriate.
differentiate: Stress testing evaluates inducible ischemia/functional capacity; coronary CT angiography evaluates anatomy and has different strengths/limitations.
A positive stress result is probability evidence, not automatic proof of obstructive epicardial CAD.
assessment: Clarify symptoms, prior CAD, resting ECG, ability to exercise, contraindications and pretest likelihood of ischemic disease.
Exclude unstable symptoms/ACS before outpatient stress testing.
workup: Select modality based on the diagnostic question and patient factors; use local cardiology/imaging pathways for intermediate-risk stable presentations.
Interpret symptoms, workload, ECG/imaging changes and test quality together rather than one line of the report.
management: High-risk or strongly positive studies require cardiology evaluation; equivocal/nondiagnostic results require a deliberate next test rather than repeating the same low-yield modality.
Low-risk reassuring results should not end evaluation when the clinical syndrome changes or another diagnosis remains likely.
medicationSafety: Rate-limiting drugs may affect exercise testing depending on the question; medication holding is test-specific and should follow instructions.
Pharmacologic stress agents have contraindications and require supervised protocols.
counselling: Explain what the test can answer and what a nondiagnostic/positive result might lead to before ordering it.
followUp: Own the result and downstream cardiology/anatomic evaluation rather than treating the stress-test report as a completed referral.
examTrap: Ordering an exercise ECG in a patient who cannot exercise adequately or has an uninterpretable baseline ECG.
oneLinePearl: The best stress test is the one that can actually answer the clinical question.

title: Echocardiography: Turn Measurements Into Hemodynamics and Clinical Meaning
bottomLine: An echocardiogram reports structure and estimated hemodynamics; the clinician must correlate EF, chamber size, valves, filling pressures, RV function and pulmonary-pressure estimates with the patient's symptoms and disease context rather than treating EF as the whole study.
recognize: Preserved EF does not exclude HF; valve disease, diastolic dysfunction, RV failure and pulmonary hypertension can cause major symptoms with normal LVEF.
A mildly reduced EF may be chronic/stable or new/significant depending on prior imaging and clinical context.
differentiate: Estimated pulmonary pressure does not establish a final pulmonary-hypertension diagnosis.
A 'normal EF' does not make dyspnea noncardiac when there is severe valve disease or abnormal filling/RV function.
assessment: Compare the echo indication with symptoms, exam, ECG, BNP/NT-proBNP and prior imaging.
Ask whether the finding explains the clinical problem and whether it changes therapy/referral.
workup: Review EF, LV/RV size/function, atrial size, valve severity, pericium and pulmonary-pressure estimates together.
Use repeat echo when a guideline-supported surveillance interval, treatment change or new clinical deterioration justifies it—not as routine annual imaging for every stable patient.
management: Refer severe valve disease, new significant ventricular dysfunction, major RV/pulmonary-pressure abnormality or unexplained structural findings appropriately.
Use echo phenotype to guide HF and valve management rather than one generic HF pathway.
medicationSafety: Avoid aggressive preload/afterload changes in severe fixed outflow obstruction or RV-dependent states without clinical context.
Do not start pulmonary vasodilators from an echo estimate alone.
counselling: Explain that EF is one component of heart function and that valve/RV/filling findings may be equally important.
followUp: Use the lesion/phenotype to define repeat imaging and specialty follow-up; compare with prior studies for true change.
examTrap: Reassuring a dyspneic patient because EF is 60% while ignoring severe mitral disease or RV dysfunction.
oneLinePearl: Read an echo as a hemodynamic story, not an EF number.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Society of Echocardiography standards

title: Cardiac CT and MRI: Choose Anatomy, Tissue, or Function With a Defined Question
bottomLine: Cardiac CT and MRI are advanced problem-solving tools, not routine upgrades from echo. CT is strong for coronary/anatomic questions; MRI excels at tissue characterization, ventricular volumes/function and selected cardiomyopathy/myocarditis/infiltrative questions. Order either only when the answer will change management.
recognize: Coronary CT angiography can evaluate coronary anatomy in selected stable patients when pretest probability and image quality are appropriate.
Cardiac MRI is valuable for myocarditis, scar/fibrosis, cardiomyopathy, infiltrative disease and complex ventricular assessment.
differentiate: CT uses ionizing radiation and often iodinated contrast; MRI avoids ionizing radiation but has device/claustrophobia/gadolinium considerations.
Neither test replaces urgent ACS evaluation in unstable chest pain.
assessment: Define the exact question, pretest probability, prior ECG/echo/stress findings, renal function, rhythm/heart rate and implant/device history.
Assess pregnancy, contrast allergy and ability to cooperate with breath-holds/scan conditions.
workup: Use CT, MRI, stress imaging or invasive angiography according to the question and local cardiology/imaging pathway.
Avoid repeating an advanced study that cannot change treatment or duplicates recent adequate imaging.
management: Act on high-risk coronary or structural findings with appropriate cardiology referral.
Use MRI phenotype to refine cardiomyopathy/myocarditis/infiltrative diagnosis and prognosis when specialist interpretation supports it.
medicationSafety: Iodinated contrast requires renal/allergy consideration; gadolinium use requires renal and agent-specific safety review.
Some implanted devices require MRI-conditional protocols rather than assuming MRI is absolutely contraindicated.
redFlags: Severe renal dysfunction when contrast-dependent test is planned
counselling: Explain what the advanced test adds beyond echo/stress testing and why a more complex scan is not automatically better.
followUp: Ensure incidental and actionable cardiac/extracardiac findings are assigned to an owner and closed-loop.
examTrap: Ordering cardiac MRI for routine stable hypertension or CT angiography in active unstable ACS instead of choosing the test for the actual question.
oneLinePearl: CT answers anatomy; MRI answers tissue and function—only order when the answer changes care.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society cardiovascular imaging standards

title: After MI: Secondary Prevention Starts Before the Patient Leaves the Hospital
bottomLine: Post-MI care is not finished after reperfusion. Secondary prevention requires antithrombotic therapy appropriate to PCI/bleeding risk, intensive lipid lowering, BP/diabetes/smoking management, evidence-based ventricular/remodelling therapy when indicated, cardiac rehabilitation and reliable early follow-up with medication access and symptom education.
recognize: The early post-ACS period carries recurrent ischemic, bleeding, HF and arrhythmia risk.
Medication nonadherence often reflects cost, complexity, adverse effects or transition failures rather than unwillingness.
differentiate: Dual antiplatelet duration and anticoagulant combinations depend on stent/ACS/bleeding/AF context and are not one universal schedule.
Beta-blocker/RAAS/MRA indications depend on EF, HF, BP and comorbidity rather than 'every MI forever'.
assessment: At transition, verify symptoms, EF/HF status, rhythm, renal function/electrolytes, bleeding, medication list, smoking, diabetes/BP/lipids and access to prescriptions/follow-up.
Confirm the patient knows which chest symptoms require emergency evaluation.
workup: Ensure post-ACS EF/structural assessment and indicated lipid/renal/electrolyte monitoring are completed.
Use recurrent symptoms to reopen ischemia/stent/arrhythmia/HF evaluation rather than attributing them to recovery.
management: Implement guideline-directed antiplatelet/anticoagulant strategy, intensive lipid lowering and other indicated disease-modifying therapy.
Refer to cardiac rehabilitation and address physical activity, diet, smoking, psychosocial recovery and return-to-work/driving questions.
Use the CCS Secondary Prevention Pathway to close discharge-to-primary-care gaps.
medicationSafety: Triple antithrombotic exposure greatly increases bleeding and requires deliberate specialist-informed duration.
Monitor renal function/potassium/BP with RAAS/MRA therapy and assess statin intolerance rather than abandoning lipid therapy after one symptom report.
counselling: Teach medication purpose, bleeding precautions, cardiac rehab value and when to call EMS for recurrent ischemic symptoms.
followUp: Arrange early post-discharge review, verify cardiac-rehab enrolment and track LDL/BP/diabetes/smoking and adherence barriers over time.
examTrap: Discharging after MI with prescriptions but no cardiac-rehab referral, medication-access check or follow-up ownership.
oneLinePearl: The MI ends in the cath lab; secondary prevention starts there.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Secondary Prevention Pathway 2025–2026
